title: Rabbi Elazar ben Dalgai
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: He is mentioned in [Mishnah Tamid, chapter 3, mishnah 8](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Tamid.3.8), where he said: "My father's household had goats on Mount Mikhvar, and they would sneeze from the smell of the incense compound." There, in the Mishnah, the reading is 'ben Dagla'i'; but in the Western (Palestinian) text the reading is 'ben Dalga'i', and so it appears in the [Jerusalem Talmud Sukkah 5:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Sukkah.5.3.4); and in [Yoma 39b](https://www.sefaria.org/Yoma.39b.13) the reading is 'ben Dolga'i', and some read there 'Rabbi Yose ben Dolga'i'.[^2]

In the newspaper "Hashkafah," year 7, issue 32, Rabbi Baruch Chuma of Jerusalem writes that he found in a Bomberg edition of the Mishnah, printed in Venice in the year 5288 [1527–1528], the text: "Rabbi Elazar said: two dalgei of goats..." etc. He conjectures that the first copyist wrote 'two dalgei izim' (taking dalgei to mean flocks), and the second copyist came and wrote 'ben Dalgei.' Hyman acknowledges it as a clever suggestion, but finds it very difficult to emend in four places. Likewise, we would also have to emend and say 'Rabbi Eliezer', since Rabbi Elazar (ben Shamua) was not in the time of the Temple; furthermore, Hyman does not find anywhere in the Talmud the word 'dalgei' used for flocks of sheep.[^1]

notes.text: The proposed reading “two dalgei of goats” takes dalgei as flocks; Hyman rejects the conjecture and says that meaning is otherwise unattested in the Talmud. His four-location objection and Elazar/Eliezer chronology argument remain his own. The year5288 spans1527–1528.

The linked Tamid has Rabbi Eliezer ben Diglai in Hebrew, with Elazar in its English translation. Yerushalmi Sukkah gives ליעזר בן דלגיי, rendered Eliezer ben Dalgai in its English translation. Yoma has Rabbi (Yose ben) Dulgai. [Heilprin’s Tamid entry](https://www.girsology.com/seder-hadorot.html?entry=511&lang=en) cites the Tamid and Yerushalmi accounts and tentatively compares the name Dola’ai. [His Yoma entry](https://www.girsology.com/seder-hadorot.html?entry=1917&lang=en) records the Yose reading. The Bomberg printing and the Hashkafah article are cited by Hyman.
